strengths: Pioneering focus on TTA for VLODs: The paper addresses an important and under-explored problem—adapting vision–language object detectors (such as YOLO-World and Grounding DINO) at test time without target annotations or source data, whereas most existing VLM-TTA work focuses solely on image classification.

Technically well-motivated formulation: Leveraging dense proposal overlap as a spatial self-consistency graph (IoU-Weighted Entropy) is a clever, domain-specific insight that directly counters confirmation bias and isolated false positives typical of vanilla entropy minimization in object detection.

Effective prompt selection strategy: Demonstrating that standard prompt averaging degrades VLOD detection performance and proposing an image-conditioned prompt selection (IPS) mechanism provides a clear, practical improvement over classification-centric VLM adaptation baselines.

Thorough and comprehensive benchmarking: The method is validated across 96 scenarios covering style transfer (Watercolor, ClipArt, Comic), driving environments (Cityscapes, BDD100K), illumination changes (ExDark), and common corruptions (PASCAL-C, COCO-C) across two distinct VLOD paradigms (CNN-based YOLO-World and Transformer-based Grounding DINO) and varying model scales.

Detailed ablation and efficiency analysis: The paper includes extensive hyperparameter sensitivity studies (IoU threshold, component exponent, fusion coefficient, prompt fraction), latency/FPS trade-off comparisons, adapter placement ablations, and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: Heuristic differences in adapter placement across architectures: The adaptation strategy requires empirical tailoring of adapter placement depending on the model architecture (vision backbone + neck for YOLO-World vs. BERT text encoder for Grounding DINO). While analyzed in Section 4.3, a unified or self-adaptive placement strategy would improve general applicability.

Limited effectiveness on small/sparse objects: As acknowledged in the limitations, the method yields smaller gains on driving datasets (Cityscapes, BDD100K) where objects are often tiny, distant, and have minimal proposal overlap, which diminishes the clustering advantage of IoU-weighted entropy.

Prompt engineering and scalability overhead: Generating and evaluating an expanded candidate pool of GPT prompts (e.g., 16 prompts per class) poses scalability challenges when extending the detector to large-vocabulary open-world settings (e.g., LVIS with 1,200+ classes), both in terms of text caching memory and similarity computation.

Graph construction complexity: Although selecting the top-$M$ proposals ($M=600$) keeps inference latency reasonable (~20 FPS vs. 22 FPS for naive adapter tuning), building the class-wise IoU connected components scales quadratically with proposal count per class ($O(M^2)$ in the worst case), which could become a bottleneck under dense multi-class scenes.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: While test-time adaptation (TTA) has been widely investigated for image classification in vision-language models, this work is among the first dedicated frameworks designed specifically for vision-language object detectors (VLODs).

Detection-tailored algorithmic formulation: Instead of naively applying classification entropy minimization, the proposed IoU-Weighted Entropy (IWE) effectively leverages the spatial redundancy of object proposals. Weighting entropy by connected component size in class-specific IoU graphs directly mitigates confirmation bias from isolated false positives.

Insightful prompt selection mechanism: The paper demonstrates that standard prompt averaging can degrade VLOD performance and proposes an image-conditioned prompt selection (IPS) strategy that ranks and filters prompt candidates based on detector proposal consensus.

Extensive and rigorous benchmarking: The approach is evaluated across 96 scenarios covering multiple domain shifts (artistic styles, driving scenes, low light, and synthetic corruptions on PASCAL-C and COCO-C) on two prominent VLOD architectures (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO), showing consistent improvements over zero-shot and competitive TTA baselines.

Comprehensive ablation and sensitivity analysis: The authors provide detailed investigations into adapter placement across vision vs. text modules, sensitivity to hyperparameters (IoU threshold, cluster exponent, prompt retention ratio), proposal filtering budgets, and latency/parameter overhead.
weaknesses: Lack of a centralized modular ablation table: While components are analyzed across several figures and appendices, the main text lacks a concise, side-by-side ablation table isolating the individual gains of IWE versus IPS across multiple benchmarks.

Performance limitations on small, dispersed objects: The core premise of IWE depends on dense proposal overlap. Consequently, gains are noticeably smaller on driving benchmarks (e.g., BDD100K and Cityscapes) where small, distant, non-overlapping objects dominate.

Inference latency overhead: Although faster than prompt-tuning baselines, adapting parameters on-the-fly via backpropagation per image drops YOLO-World throughput from 89 FPS (zero-shot) to 20 FPS, which may constrain real-time deployment.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: Vision-Language Object Detectors (VLODs) suffer from domain shifts, and adapting TTA techniques from classification to open-vocabulary detection addresses an important and under-explored gap.

Detection-specific formulation: The proposed IoU-Weighted Entropy (IWE) effectively targets the spatial redundancy in dense object detection proposals, penalizing isolated false alarms and reinforcing spatially consistent cluster detections.

Comprehensive empirical benchmark: The method is evaluated across 96 distinct test scenarios spanning artistic style shifts, autonomous driving datasets (Cityscapes, BDD100K), low-light conditions (ExDark), and corruption benchmarks (PASCAL-C, COCO-C) on two mainstream architectures (YOLO-World and Grounding DINO).

Thorough ablation studies: The submission includes detailed analyses on adapter placement, prompt generation sources, sensitivity of hyperparameters (θ, γ, λ, ρ, M), runtime/FPS overhead, and batch size effects.
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: The individual components largely adapt existing concepts—entropy minimization via adapters (TENT), learnable text prompt residuals (from DPE), and connected-component / IoU-based filtering (common in pseudo-labeling for object detection). Appendix A.1 presents a standard Euclidean-cosine identity as a formal proposition, which adds little theoretical value.

Inconsistent adaptation scheme across architectures: In YOLO-World, adapters are inserted into the visual backbone and neck, whereas in Grounding DINO, adapters are placed into the text encoder. Requiring different module placements across architectures diminishes the claim of a unified, architecture-agnostic framework.

Potential noise in Image-Conditioned Prompt Selection (IPS): The image-level prompt ranking score r_{k,t} is computed by averaging similarity over all N proposals, the vast majority of which represent background regions. Computing mean compatibility across thousands of background boxes risks diluting object-level semantic signals, especially in sparse scenes.

Marginal improvements on challenging scenes: As acknowledged in the limitations, the method yields smaller gains on datasets with many small or non-overlapping instances (e.g., Cityscapes and BDD100K), where dense spatial clustering does not naturally occur.

Hyperparameter sensitivity in unsupervised settings: The framework introduces multiple sensitive hyperparameters (IoU threshold θ, exponent γ, fusion weight λ, retention ratio ρ, top-M proposals). Setting distinct fusion weights for YOLO-World (λ=0.3) and Grounding DINO (λ=0.1) suggests manual tuning that may be difficult to generalize under genuine test-time deployment without validation labels.

strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language object detectors (VLODs) is significantly less explored than TTA for classification, despite the widespread deployment of models like YOLO-World and Grounding DINO.

Detection-tailored methodology: IoU-Weighted Entropy (IWE) effectively leverages spatial redundancy in dense object detection proposals to mitigate confirmation bias from isolated false positives, directly exploiting the spatial geometry inherent to object detectors.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The benchmarking covers two distinct detector architectures (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO) across diverse distribution shifts (artistic style shifts, adverse driving, illumination, and common corruptions in PASCAL-C and COCO-C).

Favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off: Unlike prior teacher-student approaches (e.g., TTAOD-F) that require multiple forward passes and high GPU memory, VLOD-TTA operates on a single-image, single-update setting with substantially lower memory and latency overhead.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The manuscript provides insightful analyses into architectural adapter placement differences between YOLO-World and Grounding DINO, hyperparameter sensitivity, prompt generation strategies, and failure case diagnostics (e.g., label overlap and resolution issues on Cityscapes).
weaknesses: Global proposal averaging in prompt selection: The prompt compatibility metric $r_{k,t}$ computes the average cosine similarity over all $N$ region proposals. For classes that occupy only a tiny fraction of the image or are completely absent, averaging over hundreds of background proposals could dilute the prompt selection signal. The proof in Section 6.1 merely establishes the standard equivalence between cosine similarity and Euclidean distance, rather than justifying why all proposals should be averaged.

Architecture-dependent adaptation design: The method requires adapting different modules depending on the model (vision backbone/neck for YOLO-World vs. text encoder for Grounding DINO). While the paper provides sound intuition based on cross-modal fusion points, this reduces the plug-and-play generality across arbitrary detector architectures.

Performance constraints on small objects: As noted in the driving benchmark results and the Cityscapes ablation, the IoU graph clustering struggles in scenes with many distant/small objects where proposal overlap is sparse, necessitating higher image resolutions or class merges to achieve significant gains.

Test-time latency: Although significantly faster than TTAOD-F, performing backpropagation per test image drops YOLO-World throughput from 89 FPS (zero-shot) to 20 FPS, which may still be restrictive for edge or hard real-time deployment scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), which has received significantly less attention than image classification TTA.

The core idea of IoU-weighted entropy minimization (IWE) is intuitive and well-tailored to object detection: it cleverly exploits the spatial redundancy of proposal clusters to counteract the confirmation bias of standard entropy minimization.

Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse domain shifts (artistic style, driving conditions, illumination, and common corruptions) on both CNN-based (YOLO-World) and Transformer-based (Grounding DINO) architectures.
Significantly lower memory footprint and inference latency compared to prior VLOD-TTA work (TTAOD-F), making it much more practical for online deployment.
Detailed ablation studies and honest failure-case analyses (e.g., investigating why Cityscapes proved difficult due to small objects and rider/person class overlap).
weaknesses: In Section 3.3, the prompt compatibility score $r_{k,t}$ is computed by averaging similarity over all $N$ region proposals ($r_{k,t} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N z_{i,k,t}$). Because most proposals correspond to background or other classes, averaging over all proposals could introduce significant noise, especially when class $k$ is either absent or covers only a tiny fraction of the image. The paper lacks ablation or discussion comparing this global average against pooling over top-scoring proposals.

The 'theoretical justification' referenced in Section 3.3 and presented as a formal Proposition in Section 6.1 is merely the elementary algebraic identity for unit vectors $\|\hat{\mathbf{v}} - \hat{\mathbf{e}}\|^2 = 2 - 2\hat{\mathbf{v}}^\top \hat{\mathbf{e}}$. Framing this standard cosine-Euclidean relation as a theoretical justification is an overstatement.

While faster than teacher-based multi-step frameworks like TTAOD-F, the single-image backward pass still causes a substantial throughput drop compared to zero-shot inference (e.g., from 89 FPS down to 20 FPS on YOLO-World).

strengths: Addresses a timely and under-explored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), moving beyond classification TTA and reducing reliance on heavy teacher-based architectures.

Technically sound and intuitive design: IoU-weighted entropy (IWE) effectively leverages spatial redundancy in dense object proposals to combat confirmation bias, while image-conditioned prompt selection (IPS) avoids dilution caused by naive prompt averaging.

Significantly improved efficiency compared to prior VLOD TTA state-of-the-art (TTAOD-F): achieves competitive or superior mAP on COCO-C with substantially reduced GPU memory overhead (3.76 GB vs. 11.37 GB) and faster per-image latency.

Extensive empirical benchmarking across diverse domain shifts (artistic styles, low light, autonomous driving, synthetic corruptions) on both CNN-based (YOLO-World) and Transformer-based (Grounding DINO) architectures.
Honest and insightful failure analysis and ablations, particularly regarding the challenges with small objects, resolution effects, and ambiguous class labels on Cityscapes.
weaknesses: Although faster than teacher-based alternatives, test-time backpropagation still introduces notable latency overhead (e.g., dropping YOLO-World throughput from 89 FPS to 20 FPS), which poses challenges for real-time edge deployment.

The prompt compatibility score $r_{k,t}$ in Equation (Section 3.3) averages similarity across all $N$ proposals in an image. Since the vast majority of proposals in an image correspond to background rather than category $k$, this global average could become noisy or diluted in complex scenes containing sparse foreground instances.

The method is evaluated strictly in an episodic, reset-after-prediction setting. It remains unclear how the method behaves under sequential or continual distribution shifts without resetting parameters after every image.
